questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (auxiliary verb).
questions.explanation: The subject "she" is third person singular, so the auxiliary is "doesn't" and the main verb stays in the base form.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (habit in the present).
questions.explanation: A habit in the simple present with a singular subject takes goes.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (plural subject).
options: They is playing in the park.
They am playing in the park.
They was playing in the park now.
They are playing in the park.
questions.explanation: The plural subject "they" takes "are" with the present continuous.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (subject "I").
questions.explanation: The subject "I" takes "have".

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (plural noun).
questions.explanation: The plural of child is children (irregular); it already ends in -ren.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (comparison).
options: She is more taller than me.
questions.explanation: The comparative takes "than", not "then", and "taller" is already a comparative.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (subject "each").
options: Each of the boys has a book.
Each of the boys have a book.
Each of the boys are having a book.
Each of the boy has a book.
questions.explanation: "Each" is the subject and is singular, so the verb is "has"; the noun after "of" is plural.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (verb after "did not").
questions.explanation: After "did not" the main verb is in the base form: come.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (subject "neither").
questions.explanation: "Neither" is singular, so "is" is correct.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (adjective or adverb).
questions.explanation: "Sings" is a verb and needs the adverb well; good is an adjective.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (double comparative).
options: He is more smarter than his brother.
He is smarter than his brother.
He is smarter then his brother.
He is most smarter than his brother.
questions.explanation: Use either -er or more, never both, and use "than" in a comparison.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (uncountable noun "news").
questions.explanation: "News" is an uncountable noun that takes a singular verb.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (verb "agree").
questions.explanation: "Agree" is a verb; "am agree" is wrong.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (told or said).
options: She said me that she was late.
She told that she was late me.
She says me she was late.
She told me that she was late.
questions.explanation: "Tell" takes an object (told me); "say" does not.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (uncountable noun "furniture").
questions.explanation: "Furniture" is uncountable and takes a singular verb; it has no plural form.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence ("look forward to").
options: I look forward to meet you.
I look forward to meeting you.
I look forward for meeting you.
I am look forward to meeting you.
questions.explanation: In "look forward to", "to" is a preposition and is followed by an -ing form.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence ("the reason is").
options: The reason is because he was late.
The reason is that he was late.
The reason is for he was late.
The reason being because he was late.
questions.explanation: "The reason is because" is redundant; use "the reason is that".

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence ("despite").
options: Despite the rain, we went out.
Despite of the rain, we went out.
Despite from the rain, we went out.
In despite of the rain, we went out.
questions.explanation: "Despite" is not followed by "of"; the alternative is "in spite of the rain".

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (reported question).
options: She asked me that where I lived.
She asked me where did I live.
She asked me where do I live.
She asked me where I lived.
questions.explanation: A reported question takes statement word order, with no "that".

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence (neither-nor).
options: Neither Ravi nor his friends is coming.
Neither Ravi nor his friends was coming.
Neither Ravi nor his friends are coming.
Neither Ravi nor his friends has coming.
questions.explanation: With neither-nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "his friends" (plural), so "are".
